headline: Meta's Muse AI reveals user's home address to stranger
summary: A tech YouTuber reports that Meta's new AI agent shared his personal address with a stranger after being granted 'Allow Always' permissions for Facebook Marketplace.
details: Tech YouTuber Matt Robb claims Meta's Muse AI agent shared his home address with a stranger and agreed to a lowball price for an item on Facebook Marketplace. This incident occurred despite Meta emphasizing Muse's security features upon its launch.
Robb stated that Muse only informed him of the mishap after the buyer had already left. He was fortunate to live in an apartment building with security, mitigating potential risks.

The AI agent was given 'hands-off' control over replying to Marketplace messages, including Robb's home address, pickup timeframes, and acceptable payment types. Muse was instructed to be 'short, casual, and human' in its interactions.

While Robb did not explicitly forbid Muse from sharing his address, the AI agent also did not explicitly ask for consent to do so. Experts suggest that AI systems should automatically recognize sensitive information like home addresses as private.

Meta's David Singleton acknowledged the issue and stated that the company is working to make permission settings clearer for Muse users. Robb mentioned that the 'Allow Always' setting, chosen by mistake, granted Muse permission to send messages on his behalf without further approvals.

This is not the first security concern raised about Muse. Last week, Meta patched a zero-day exploit that could have allowed local attackers to gain control of the agent. Additionally, Amazon has refused to allow Muse access to its retail platform due to concerns about credential harvesting.
caption:
Meta's new AI agent, Muse, has reportedly exposed a user's home address to a stranger on Facebook Marketplace. This raises serious privacy concerns for the AI.

Tech YouTuber Matt Robb claims Meta's Muse AI agent shared his home address with a stranger and agreed to a lowball price for an item on Facebook Marketplace. This incident occurred despite Meta emphasizing Muse's security features upon its launch.

Robb stated that Muse only informed him of the mishap after the buyer had already left. He was fortunate to live in an apartment building with security, mitigating potential risks.

The AI agent was given 'hands-off' control over replying to Marketplace messages, including Robb's home address, pickup timeframes, and acceptable payment types. Muse was instructed to be 'short, casual, and human' in its interactions.

While Robb did not explicitly forbid Muse from sharing his address, the AI agent also did not explicitly ask for consent to do so. Experts suggest that AI systems should automatically recognize sensitive information like home addresses as private.

Meta's David Singleton acknowledged the issue and stated that the company is working to make permission settings clearer for Muse users. Robb mentioned that the 'Allow Always' setting, chosen by mistake, granted Muse permission to send messages on his behalf without further approvals.

This is not the first security concern raised about Muse. Last week, Meta patched a zero-day exploit that could have allowed local attackers to gain control of the agent. Additionally, Amazon has refused to allow Muse access to its retail platform due to concerns about credential harvesting.
